concept.name: Distributed Cron & Scheduling

relationships.description: Connects Distributed Cron & Scheduling to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Distributed cron and scheduling systems execute time-based and delayed jobs reliably across a fleet of stateless workers without single-point-of-failure downtime or duplicate runs.
spark.keyTakeaway: Decouple time-trigger evaluation from job execution, shard triggers across partitioned queues or hash rings, and enforce idempotency keys at the worker boundary.

concept.whyItMatters: A single-host `crontab` fails silently when the VM reboots, cannot scale past one machine's CPU, and offers no visibility into missed or overlapping runs. Distributed scheduling ensures millions of recurring and delayed tasks (billing runs, digest emails, retry timers) fire accurately even during node crashes, rolling deployments, and traffic spikes.
whenToUse: Executing recurring business workflows (daily invoicing, hourly data compaction, subscription renewals) with high availability and audit logs.
Managing millions of per-user delayed tasks (e.g., 'send reminder 24 hours after signup') where in-memory timers would be lost on restart.
Coordinating fleet-wide periodic jobs with strict concurrency policies (forbid overlap, replace stale runs, or catch up missed windows).
whenNotToUse: Sub-second reactive event processing where a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) should trigger workers immediately upon event arrival.
Simple single-instance background polling inside a monolith where a single `cron` or in-process ticker with no HA requirement suffices.
Complex multi-step DAGs with dynamic data dependencies better served by a dedicated workflow orchestrator like Temporal or Apache Airflow.
keyPoints: At-least-once delivery is the practical standard in distributed scheduling; exactly-once execution is achieved by pairing at-least-once dispatch with idempotent workers (`job_id + scheduled_epoch`).
PostgreSQL `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` works reliably up to ~5,000–10,000 jobs/sec when indexed on `(status, next_run_at)`.

High-scale schedulers (100,000+ timers/sec) partition schedules by time-bucket or consistent-hashed shard keys and use Hierarchical Timing Wheels (`O(1)` insert/tick) in memory backed by durable WALs.
Deterministic jitter (`hash(job_id) % window_sec`) spreads `:00` minute-boundary spikes smoothly without breaking cron semantics.
Explicit `concurrencyPolicy` (`Allow`, `Forbid`, `Replace`) and `misfirePolicy` (skip vs. backfill) prevent cascading queues when jobs run slower than their interval.

examples.title: Sharded PostgreSQL Scheduler for SaaS Webhooks
examples.scenario: A platform schedules 40,000 recurring customer report jobs, 80% of which are configured for `0 0 * * *` (midnight UTC). Workers previously locked the whole table, causing 12-second DB stalls.
examples.outcome: Adding a `jitter_sec = hashtext(job_id) % 300` offset and polling with `UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= now() ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)` eliminated lock contention and smoothed midnight CPU load by 5x.

examples.title: Kubernetes CronJob with `Forbid` Concurrency
examples.scenario: An ETL sync `CronJob` runs every 5 minutes (`*/5 * * * *`). A downstream warehouse slowdown causes the 10:00 UTC pod to take 8 minutes.
examples.outcome: With `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` and `startingDeadlineSeconds: 120`, Kubernetes skips the 10:05 tick cleanly instead of launching a competing pod that would corrupt incremental checkpoints.

tradeOffs.factor: Relational DB Polling (`SKIP LOCKED`) vs. Partitioned Time-Wheels (Kafka / Redis ZSET)
tradeOffs.pro: SQL polling provides transactional state transitions, rich ad-hoc querying, and zero extra infrastructure up to ~10k jobs/sec.
tradeOffs.con: Frequent `UPDATE` and index scans create MVCC bloat and vacuum pressure in PostgreSQL at high timer churn, where partitioned timing wheels scale far better.

tradeOffs.factor: Centralized Leader Dispatcher vs. Shared-Nothing Partitioned Workers
tradeOffs.pro: A single leader (via Raft/etcd lease) simplifies global rate limiting and concurrency checks across all jobs.
tradeOffs.con: A single dispatcher becomes a throughput bottleneck and introduces a failover pause (5–30 s) when the leader crashes.

tradeOffs.pro: Backfilling missed ticks guarantees no billing or compliance window is skipped after a 2-hour outage.
tradeOffs.con: Replaying hundreds of missed ticks simultaneously on recovery can overwhelm downstream databases unless capped by a backfill rate limit.

failureModes.name: Midnight / Top-of-Hour Thundering Herd
failureModes.description: Users disproportionately pick `0 * * * *` or `0 0 * * *`, causing 100x normal load at `:00` seconds and exhausting worker pools and DB connections.
failureModes.mitigation: Inject deterministic hash-based jitter (e.g., 0–60 s) into `next_run_at` or enforce per-tenant dispatch rate limits.

failureModes.name: Split-Brain Duplicate Execution
failureModes.description: A scheduler leader loses its heartbeat due to a network blip while a new leader takes over; both dispatch the `10:00:00` job instance.
failureModes.mitigation: Insert a unique execution record (`PRIMARY KEY (job_id, scheduled_epoch)`) before running the job, or pass an idempotency key to downstream APIs.

failureModes.name: Slow-Job Pileup (Unbounded Overlap)
failureModes.description: A job scheduled every 60 s begins taking 90 s due to degraded dependencies, spawning overlapping workers until memory or connection pools exhaust.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` (skip if active) or `Replace` (cancel stale run), and set hard execution timeouts.

failureModes.name: Daylight Saving Time (DST) & Timezone Drift
failureModes.description: A job scheduled for `02:30 America/New_York` is skipped entirely on spring-forward day or runs twice on fall-back day.
failureModes.mitigation: Store all internal trigger timestamps in UTC, explicitly document per-job timezone rules, and record the logical `scheduled_epoch` to deduplicate fall-back repeats.

commonMistakes: Using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` without `SKIP LOCKED`, causing worker threads to block behind each other on the same due rows.
Storing `next_run_at` in local server time instead of UTC, causing silent skips or double-fires during DST transitions.
Ignoring worker crash recovery—leaving jobs stuck in `RUNNING` forever because no `lease_expires_at` reaper exists.
Coupling the scheduler's tick loop directly to synchronous job execution so one slow HTTP call stalls all subsequent timers.
Failing to set a `startingDeadlineSeconds` or misfire cap, resulting in a storm of stale jobs firing hours after an outage.

sections.content:
## The idea

A distributed scheduler turns wall-clock expressions (like `0 9 * * 1-5`) and one-off delays into reliable, fault-tolerant executions across a cluster of machines. The core design principle is **separating scheduling from execution**: a durable **Schedule Store** tracks job definitions and next trigger times, a **Dispatcher** claims due triggers using atomic leases or partitioned ownership, and stateless **Workers** execute the payload asynchronously.

Because network partitions and process crashes make true distributed exactly-once delivery impossible, production schedulers aim for **at-least-once dispatch + idempotent execution**. Every trigger produces a deterministic execution ID—typically `(job_id, scheduled_timestamp_utc)`—so even if two dispatchers race during a failover, only one execution record commits or has side effects.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a recurring daily digest job (`job_id = "digest-42"`, cron `0 8 * * *`, timezone `Asia/Kolkata`, `concurrencyPolicy = Forbid`) through a sharded database scheduler:

1. **Schedule Registration**: The control plane computes `next_run_at = 2026-11-13T02:30:00Z` (08:00 IST) plus deterministic jitter `+17 s` (`2026-11-13T02:30:17Z`) and writes the row with `state = IDLE`.
2. **Atomic Claim**: At `02:30:17Z`, Dispatcher Pod 2 runs `SELECT id FROM schedules WHERE state = 'IDLE' AND next_run_at <= now() ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 50 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
3. **Idempotent Enqueue & Advance**: Inside the same DB transaction, Pod 2 inserts `(job_id='digest-42', scheduled_at='2026-11-13T02:30:17Z')` into `job_runs` (unique constraint prevents duplicates), updates `next_run_at` to `2026-11-14T02:30:17Z`, sets `lease_expires_at = now() + 60s`, and pushes the task ID to a Kafka/SQS worker queue.
4. **Worker Execution & Heartbeat**: A worker pops the task, verifies `job_runs.status == 'QUEUED'`, flips it to `'RUNNING'`, sends the email batch, and marks it `'SUCCEEDED'`.
5. **Crash Recovery**: If the worker crashes mid-run, a reaper scans `job_runs WHERE status = 'RUNNING' AND lease_expires_at < now()` every 15 s and re-queues the task up to `max_retries = 3`.

data.caption: Decoupling atomic trigger claiming from queued execution prevents slow jobs from stalling the scheduler's clock.

sections.content:
## Scaling beyond single-table polling

A single PostgreSQL table with `SKIP LOCKED` handles up to ~5,000–10,000 triggers/sec cleanly, but beyond that, continuous `UPDATE`s on `next_run_at` cause B-tree index bloat and autovacuum saturation. High-scale systems (like Temporal, Uber's Cherami, or cloud timer services) solve this with **time-bucketed sharding**.

Triggers are partitioned by `(shard_id, time_bucket)`—for example, 1-minute buckets hashed across 64 shards. Each shard owner loads only the upcoming 1–5 minutes of timers into an in-memory **Hierarchical Timing Wheel**, where inserting or expiring a timer is $O(1)$ regardless of total pending timers. When a bucket finishes, the shard advances its durable checkpoint cursor in storage.

## Comparing distributed scheduling architectures

| Architecture | Max Throughput | Trigger Precision | Operational Complexity | Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **SQL `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`** | ~5k–10k jobs/sec | 1–5 s (poll interval) | Low (reuses existing RDBMS) | Quartz (tuned), PgBoss, River |
| **Redis `ZSET` (`ZRANGEBYSCORE`)** | ~50k+ jobs/sec | < 100 ms | Medium (Lua scripts + AOF persistence) | Sidekiq, BullMQ, Celery Beat |
| **Partitioned Timing Wheel + WAL** | 100k–1M+ timers/sec | 10–100 ms | High (shard rebalancing, cursor checkpoints) | Temporal Timers, HashedWheelTimer |
| **Control-Plane Cron Controller** | ~100s–1k jobs/min | 10–60 s | Low in K8s (built-in controller) | Kubernetes `CronJob`, Nomad Periodic |

## Failure modes

- **Unbounded Misfire Storm**: After a 4-hour outage, a scheduler configured to backfill every missed 1-minute tick fires 240 runs per job simultaneously. *Mitigation*: Cap backfill windows (`startingDeadlineSeconds`), rate-limit catch-up dispatches, or default non-critical jobs to `Skip`.
- **Zombie Execution After Worker OOM**: A worker is `SIGKILL`ed mid-job, leaving the run stuck in `RUNNING` forever. *Mitigation*: Require periodic lease extensions (e.g., every 15 s) and run a background reaper to re-queue expired leases.
- **Clock Skew Across Dispatchers**: Node A's clock is 4 s ahead of Node B's, causing early triggers or inconsistent lease expirations. *Mitigation*: Use the database's `now()` as the single source of time truth for SQL schedulers, and monitor NTP offset alerts (`> 100 ms`).
- **Hot-Key Contention at `:00` Boundaries**: Thousands of cron jobs share `0 * * * *`, saturating connection pools at the top of every hour. *Mitigation*: Add deterministic per-job jitter (`hash(job_id) % 60`) and pre-warm worker autoscaling.

## Idempotency and observability

Because any network timeout between a dispatcher and queue can cause a duplicate enqueue, workers must treat the `run_id` (`job_id + scheduled_epoch`) as a first-class **idempotency key**. Downstream mutations should record `run_id` in a unique constraint or pass it in `Idempotency-Key` HTTP headers.

For observability, track **schedule lag** (`actual_start_time - scheduled_time`) at p99, **active lease count**, **misfire rate**, and **dead-letter queue depth**. A rising p99 schedule lag is the earliest leading indicator that dispatcher polling or worker concurrency is saturated.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Store all `next_run_at` timestamps in UTC and evaluate cron expressions with an explicit IANA timezone (e.g., `Asia/Kolkata`) to handle DST safely.
- [ ] Generate a deterministic `run_id` (`job_id + scheduled_epoch`) and enforce uniqueness before side effects occur.
- [ ] Configure explicit `concurrencyPolicy` (`Forbid`, `Replace`, or `Allow`) and `misfirePolicy` (`Skip` vs. bounded `Backfill`) on every job.
- [ ] Add deterministic hash jitter (`0–60 s`) for non-precision-critical `:00` cron jobs to flatten top-of-hour spikes.
- [ ] Implement a lease-expiration reaper and monitor p99 `schedule_lag_seconds` alongside dead-lettered runs.

interviewProblems.title: Distributed Cron & Scheduling
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Distributed Cron & Scheduling. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Distributed cron and scheduling systems execute time-based and delayed jobs reliably across a fleet of stateless workers without single-point-of-failure downtime or duplicate runs.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Task Queue applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Stateless Workers.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Stateless Workers experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Inject deterministic hash-based jitter (e.g., 0–60 s) into `next_run_at` or enforce per-tenant dispatch rate limits.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Decouple time-trigger evaluation from job execution, shard triggers across partitioned queues or hash rings, and enforce idempotency keys at the worker boundary.
Avoid trap: Using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` without `SKIP LOCKED`, causing worker threads to block behind each other on the same due rows.
Avoid trap: Storing `next_run_at` in local server time instead of UTC, causing silent skips or double-fires during DST transitions.
When to reach for it: Executing recurring business workflows (daily invoicing, hourly data compaction, subscription renewals) with high availability and audit logs.
When to reach for it: Managing millions of per-user delayed tasks (e.g., 'send reminder 24 hours after signup') where in-memory timers would be lost on restart.

putItTogether.title: Putting Distributed Scheduling Cron Together
putItTogether.summary: Decouple time-trigger evaluation from job execution, shard triggers across partitioned queues or hash rings, and enforce idempotency keys at the worker boundary.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Distributed Scheduling Cron before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Adding a `jitter_sec = hashtext(job_id) % 300` offset and polling with `UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= now() ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)` eliminated lock contention and smoothed midnight CPU load by 5x.
